Description: A long biographical tomb inscription of Weni, a Sixth Dynasty court official who served kings Teti, Pepi I, and Merenre I. Carved on a large limestone slab from his tomb at Abydos, it is the longest surviving biographical text from the Old Kingdom. It records his investigation of a harem conspiracy, his quarrying and canal work at the First Cataract, and five military campaigns against the 'Sand-Dwellers' of Sinai and southern Canaan, with an army drawn from Egypt, Nubia, and Libya.
Interpretations: Weni gives the earliest detailed Egyptian account of campaigning in the Sinai-Canaan region and shows Egypt already projecting power into the land later promised to Abraham centuries before the patriarchs. His 'Sand-Dwellers' are a general term for desert nomads, not Israelites, and the inscription says nothing about the patriarchs; it illuminates the world of the early second millennium BC, not a specific biblical event.
AlternativeNames: Inscription of Weni; Autobiography of Uni
BiblicalSignificance: It illuminates the Egyptian-Canaanite world of the third millennium BC in which the earliest biblical history is set, showing Egyptian armies already operating in Canaan long before Israel existed as a nation.
